title: Range Module
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking every individual number directly versus a sorted list of merged, non-overlapping ranges.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a Range Module that tracks ranges of numbers, supporting addRange(left, right), which adds the half-open range [left, right) to the tracked numbers; queryRange(left, right), which returns true only if every number in [left, right) is currently being tracked; and removeRange(left, right), which stops tracking every number in [left, right).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of addRange, removeRange, and queryRange calls"],["Output","The result of every queryRange call"],["Goal","Support all three operations efficiently, even over a huge numeric range"],["Constraints","0 <= left < right <= 10^9; up to 10000 calls total"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The tracked numbers form contiguous ranges, over a potentially huge domain","Represent tracked numbers as a sorted list of merged, non-overlapping ranges, not individual numbers"],["Ranges must be merged (on add) or split (on remove) at their boundaries","Binary search to quickly find which existing ranges are affected by a new operation"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Maintain a set of tracked numbers, described compactly as ranges rather than individual values (since the domain can be up to a billion). Support adding a range (merging with anything it overlaps or touches), removing a range (splitting any overlapping range at the boundary), and querying whether an entire range is fully tracked.

blocks.title: Analogy: Managing Which Sections of a Highway Are Under Construction
blocks.text: Picture tracking which stretches of a very long highway are currently closed for construction. Instead of marking every individual mile marker, it is far more efficient to store just the list of closed STRETCHES, merging newly closed sections into existing ones, and splitting a stretch when part of it reopens.

blocks.caption: Keeping ranges merged and sorted lets binary search find affected ranges directly

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: addRange(10,20), removeRange(14,16), queryRange(10,14), queryRange(13,15), queryRange(16,17)

After adding [10,20) and removing [14,16), the tracked ranges become [10,14) and [16,20). queryRange(10,14) is true (fully within [10,14)); queryRange(13,15) is false (15 falls in the removed gap); queryRange(16,17) is true (fully within [16,20)).
5. How Should We Think?
Before tracking every individual number, notice that tracked numbers naturally form contiguous ranges, and operations only ever need to touch the ranges near the operation's boundaries.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Maintaining a sorted list of merged, non-overlapping ranges is a compact representation regardless of how large the numeric domain is.

Observation 2: Adding a range only affects existing ranges that overlap or touch it; everything else in the list stays untouched.

Observation 3: Removing a range only affects existing ranges that overlap it, potentially splitting one into two pieces (if the removed range sits strictly inside it) or trimming an edge.

Observation 4: A query only needs to check whether some single existing range fully contains the queried range, findable directly since the list is sorted.
This leads to representing tracked numbers as a sorted list of ranges, and implementing each operation as a scan (or binary search) that only touches the handful of ranges actually affected.
6. Brute Force Solution

Conceptually, track every individual number using a set. addRange inserts every number in the range; removeRange deletes every number in the range; queryRange checks every number in the range is present.
Step by step algorithm

items: Maintain a set of every individually tracked number.
addRange(left, right): insert every integer from left to right minus 1 into the set.
removeRange(left, right): delete every integer from left to right minus 1 from the set.
queryRange(left, right): check that every integer from left to right minus 1 is present in the set.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: track and manipulate every individual number directly

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every operation directly touches every individual number in its range, using a hash set for membership.
This is correct, but with ranges potentially spanning up to a billion numbers, iterating over every one is completely impractical.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(right minus left) per operation, potentially up to a billion per call.
Space: O(total tracked numbers), potentially enormous.
Limitation: tracked numbers are almost always contiguous, so representing and manipulating them one at a time is wildly wasteful; a range-based representation is required for the given constraints.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why tracking individual numbers is unnecessary: tracked (or untracked) numbers naturally group into contiguous ranges, and an operation on a range only interacts with a handful of EXISTING ranges near its boundaries.

What structure captures this compactly: a sorted list of merged, non-overlapping [start, end) ranges.

How addRange works: find every existing range that overlaps or touches [left, right), merge them all together with the new range into one combined range, and replace them with that single merged range.

How removeRange works: find every existing range that overlaps [left, right), and for each, keep whatever portion falls outside [left, right), which may split one range into two, trim one edge, or remove it entirely.

How queryRange works: find whether some single existing range fully contains [left, right).

The core idea: maintain a sorted list of merged ranges, and implement each operation by scanning (or binary searching) only the ranges actually affected.

Keep tracked numbers as a sorted list of non-overlapping ranges. For addRange, merge every overlapping or touching range with the new one into a single combined range. For removeRange, keep only the portions of overlapping ranges that fall outside the removed range, splitting where needed. For queryRange, check whether one existing range fully contains the query.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for addRange(10,20), removeRange(14,16)

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: merge on add, split on remove, check containment on query

blocks.text: Why This Works

Keeping ranges merged and sorted means addRange only needs to absorb the handful of existing ranges that overlap or touch the new one, replacing them with a single combined range. removeRange only needs to trim or split the handful of ranges overlapping the removed portion, keeping whatever falls outside it. queryRange only needs to find whether one existing range fully covers the query, since ranges never overlap each other. None of these operations ever need to look at, or touch, ranges far from the operation's boundaries.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per operation, where n is the number of currently stored ranges (O(log n) to locate the boundary with binary search, though a full scan is also acceptable given the constraints).
Space: O(n) for the stored ranges, always at most proportional to the number of operations performed.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Range Module is a strong example of representing state compactly by its STRUCTURE (contiguous ranges) rather than its raw contents (individual numbers), a technique essential whenever the domain is far too large to enumerate directly.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting these are half-open ranges [left, right), which affects exactly how touching (not overlapping) ranges should be merged or split.
Not correctly splitting a range into TWO pieces when a removal falls strictly inside it.
Breaking early in queryRange incorrectly, missing that only one single range needs to fully contain the query, not multiple ranges combined.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating that the domain size (up to a billion) rules out tracking individual numbers, and that ranges must be the unit of storage, sets up the correct approach immediately.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "the range can be up to a billion, how do you track it", think: store merged, non-overlapping ranges, not individual numbers.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you speed up finding the affected ranges using binary search instead of a linear scan?
How would you support a "count total tracked numbers" query efficiently?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any interval-merging problem (like Merge Intervals) applied here in a dynamic, repeatedly-updated setting.
Segment trees over compressed coordinates, an alternative structure for the same kind of range tracking, often used when queries need to be even faster.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(right - left) time per operation, up to 10^9. The optimized merged-range-list approach runs in O(n) time per operation, where n is the number of stored ranges, independent of the numeric domain.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: representing tracked state as a sorted list of merged, non-overlapping ranges instead of individual values.

Core Idea: addRange merges overlapping/touching ranges into one; removeRange keeps only the portions outside the removed range, splitting where needed; queryRange checks for a single fully-containing range.
Time: O(right - left) per operation for the brute force, O(n) (number of stored ranges) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(total tracked numbers) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: tracked numbers are naturally contiguous; storing ranges instead of individual values makes every operation independent of the domain size.
Interview Difficulty: the range-splitting and merging logic requires careful boundary handling, but the core idea is a natural fit once the domain size rules out per-number tracking.
One line memory trick: store merged ranges, not numbers; merge on add, split on remove.
